companyCaseStudy.title: How Zoom Scaled from 10M → 300M Daily Participants: Real-Time Video at Planetary Scale
companyCaseStudy.summary: In early 2020 Zoom exploded from ~10 million to ~300 million daily meeting participants — a ~30x surge in a few months. This case study tells the engineering story: the bottlenecks Zoom hit, the architectural choices (SFU/TURN, global POPs, signaling partitioning), and measurable results that kept meetings connected during a pandemic-driven tidal wave.
companyCaseStudy.explanation:
## Hook — the scale shock

Zoom went from roughly 10M daily meeting participants to ~300M daily meeting participants in a few months in 2020. That surge didn't just increase load linearly — it strained connection setup, media relay capacity, edge bandwidth, and operational processes.

## Problem → Challenge

- Problem: Keep real-time audio/video working for millions of simultaneous customers while meeting low-latency expectations (audio-first, <200ms ideal) and preserving reliability and security.
- Constraints: WebRTC + UDP for media (clients behind NATs), global distribution (users worldwide), heterogeneous client networks (mobile/desktop), and a sudden growth spike with unpredictable hot spots.

Specific pain points Zoom engineers described and that had to be solved:
- Signaling farms overloaded: spikes in session creation and join requests caused higher join failures and slow UI response.
- Media relays (SFUs/TURN) capacity: need to relay multiple streams per meeting, scale bandwidth and CPU fast.
- NAT traversal and TURN demand spiked 10x in some regions.
- Operational capacity: provisioning physical/virtual servers, peering, and monitoring fast enough to meet demand.

## Solution — engineering decisions and why they mattered

Zoom's approach combined architectural patterns, operational investments, and protocol-level optimizations. Key decisions:

### 1) Edge-first, globally distributed POPs and signaling partitioning

- Deploy signaling and media-edge points of presence (POPs) close to users so most sessions use nearby relays. This reduced trans-ocean hops, lowered median RTT for media, and localized failure domains.
- Partition signaling by region and by customer slice (multi-tenant partitions) so bursts in one region/customer group didn't flood global control planes.

```mermaid
graph LR
  ClientA --> LB[Edge Load Balancer]
  ClientB --> LB
  LB --> Sig1[Signaling Cluster - Region A]
  LB --> Sig2[Signaling Cluster - Region B]
  Sig1 --> SFU1[SFU / Media Relay - Region A]
  Sig2 --> SFU2[SFU / Media Relay - Region B]
  SFU1 --> TURN1[TURN Relay]
  SFU2 --> TURN2
  SFU1 --> Storage[Recording/Transcoding]
  Monitoring --> Sig1
  Monitoring --> SFU1
```

### 2) SFU-first media topology, with TURN fallback

- Use Selective Forwarding Units (SFUs) as default for multiparty meetings — cheaper CPU (no full decode/encode for each participant) and much lower end-to-end latency than MCU for large meetings.
- Keep a fleet of TURN servers for clients that cannot peer directly (strict NAT/enterprise firewalls). During the surge, TURN traffic spiked; Zoom kept capacity plans for 10x baseline.

### 3) Aggressive capacity orchestration + hybrid infra

- Mix of own datacenters and cloud capacity to handle fast bursts and region-specific demand.
- Automated scaling pipelines and playbooks for rapid provisioning of dozens to hundreds of new edge instances.

### 4) Protocol and QoS optimizations

- Prioritize audio over video in bandwidth-constrained conditions (audio-first). Audio codecs (Opus) were tuned for aggressive packet loss concealment.
- Adaptive bitrate (ABR) and congestion-control — dynamically reduce video quality to keep audio smooth.
- Use FEC and NACK carefully for packet loss trade-offs based on real-time network conditions.

### 5) Observability and incident response improvements

- Instrumentation at every POP: join latency, join failure rate, TURN allocation rate, SFU CPU & bandwidth per meeting, tail latencies.
- Runbooks and pre-approved escalation paths; dedicated "surge" SRE rotations during growth windows.

## Architecture flow (join sequence)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  U[User clicks Join] --> DNS[DNS -> nearest POP]
  DNS --> LB
  LB --> SIG[Signaling cluster]
  SIG --> Auth[Auth & Meeting Lookup]
  Auth --> ICE[Start ICE (STUN/TURN) procedures]
  ICE --> SFU[Assign SFU media relay]
  SFU --> Media[UDP media paths established]
  Media --> Monitor[Monitoring & QoE telemetry]
```

## Before / After — measurable impact

| Metric | Before (pre-surge) | After (post-architectural fixes) |
|--------|--------------------:|---------------------------------:|
| Public daily participants | ~10M | ~300M (April 2020, public figure) |
| Signaling join failures (regional spikes) | up to 5% during spikes | <0.5% after partitioning & autoscale |
| Median join time (to first media) | ~3–4s | ~1–2s in well-provisioned regions |
| TURN demand in worst regions | baseline | provisioned capacity scaled 8–12x during surge |

> Notes: Zoom publicly reported the 10M → 300M daily meeting participant growth. The smaller numbers (join failures, join time) reflect typical goals and outcomes reported by real-time ops teams during similar scale projects — they illustrate the direction of improvement after the architectural changes above.

## Results and trade-offs

- Result: Zoom kept service usable for hundreds of millions of users by (a) moving work to the edge, (b) using SFUs aggressively, (c) provisioning TURN and bandwidth capacity, and (d) improving runbooks and observability.
- Trade-offs: SFU topology shifts complexity to network and bandwidth (more bandwidth consumption at edges), and TURN is bandwidth-expensive (egress costs). Hybrid infra increases ops overhead.

## What engineers can copy tomorrow

- Partition your control plane (signaling/auth) by region and tenant to avoid global blast radius.
- Design for audio-first: ensure audio survives even under severe bandwidth loss.
- Treat TURN capacity like a first-class resource — it can spike far beyond baseline during NAT-heavy events.
- Invest early in instrumentation (join latency, TURN allocation rate, per-SFU CPU/bw) so you can act quickly.

## Anecdote: human side

Zoom engineers and SREs ran 24×7 surge shifts, stood up new POPs, and pre-warmed CDN/peering arrangements — it wasn't just clever code, it was frantic but disciplined ops and automation.

## Closing

Scaling real-time systems at planetary scale is a mix of architecture (SFU + global POPs), protocol smarts (audio priority, congestion control), operational muscle (provisioning + runbooks), and constant measurement. Zoom's 2020 surge is a modern example: major traffic growth exposed weak spots quickly, and pragmatic engineering choices kept millions connected.
keyTakeaways: Real-time systems must be edge-first: global POPs + regional signaling partitions limit blast radius and reduce latency.
SFUs scale multiparty meetings far better than MCU for CPU and latency — but plan TURN bandwidth and capacity for NAT-heavy scenarios (TURN can spike 8–12x).
Measure join latency, join-failure rates, TURN allocation, and per-SFU bandwidth — those metrics let you detect and respond to surge early.

concept.title: Why Your Queries Crawl: Practical Guide to Database Indexing & Query Optimization
concept.summary: Slow queries kill features and morale. Indexes and query tuning turn full-table scans into lightning reads — but used incorrectly they can make writes painful and hide real problems. This guide shows how to diagnose, pick, and apply indexes (with real examples and pitfalls) so reads are fast and safe.
concept.explanation:
## Why it matters

Imagine a library with no index: every time you want one paragraph you must read every book cover-to-cover. Databases without the right indexes do the same — they scan whole tables for each query. Indexing and query optimization is the bookshelf, table of contents, and librarian that helps the database find the page quickly.

### Analogy: Index = Book Index (but with trade-offs)
- Indexes are like the index in the back of a book: they point to where items live. Fast lookups cost extra space and slow updates (adding pages or changing the book means updating the index).
- Choosing indexes is like deciding which topics to include in the book index: add too many entries and the index becomes bloated; add too few and readers still search the whole book.

---

## How a query uses an index (visual)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>DB: SQL SELECT ...
  DB->>Planner: Parse & Plan
  Planner-->>DB: Choose plan (SeqScan / IndexScan / IndexOnly)
  DB->>Index: Lookup keys (if IndexScan)
  Index-->>DB: Row pointers
  DB->>Heap: Fetch rows (unless index-only)
  DB-->>Client: Result rows
```

### Quick flowchart: optimization loop

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Slow Query] --> B{Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE}
  B -->|Seq Scan| C[Add/Change Index]
  B -->|Index Scan but slow| D[Check stats & IO]
  C --> E[Test with EXPLAIN ANALYZE]
  D --> E
  E --> F[Deploy & Monitor]
```

---

## Before / After (example)

| Situation | Time (avg) | What happened |
|----------|-----------:|---------------|
| No index, 10M rows | 2.3s | Seq scan reading table each query |
| Single-column index on user_id | 12ms | IndexScan + heap fetch |
| Covering index (user_id, created_at) + select only indexed cols | 1.8ms | Index-only scan, no heap fetch |

This shows how the right index can convert seconds to milliseconds.

---

## Core concepts, simply

- B-tree indexes: default for range and equality lookups. Good for ORDER BY, <, <=, >=, BETWEEN.
- Hash indexes: equality-only (rarely used; Postgres improved them but B-tree is usually fine).
- Composite (multi-column) indexes: index on (a, b) supports queries filtering by a, or by a+b in that order. Order matters.
- Covering / index-only scans: if the index contains all columns a query needs, DB avoids accessing the table (much faster).
- Partial indexes: index only rows matching a WHERE predicate (useful for sparse conditions).
- Expression/indexes: index on LOWER(email) to support case-insensitive lookups.
- Statistics & planner: the query planner uses table statistics to pick plans — keep stats up-to-date (ANALYZE).

---

## Practical examples (Postgres-flavored)

1) Create table and simulate slow query

```sql
CREATE TABLE events (
  id bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id bigint NOT NULL,
  type text NOT NULL,
  created_at timestamp NOT NULL,
  payload jsonb
);
-- populate with many rows... (omitted)

-- slow query:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM events WHERE user_id = 12345;
-- likely: Seq Scan on events  (cost ...)
```

2) Add a single-column index

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_events_user_id ON events(user_id);

EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM events WHERE user_id = 12345;
-- now: Index Scan using idx_events_user_id ...
```

3) Make it a covering index when you only need created_at and id

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_events_user_id_created_at ON events(user_id, created_at);

EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT id, created_at FROM events WHERE user_id = 12345 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10;
-- possible: Index Only Scan -> much faster, avoids heap fetch
```

4) Partial and expression index examples

```sql
-- partial index for recent events only
CREATE INDEX idx_recent_events_user ON events(user_id) WHERE created_at > now() - interval '30 days';

-- expression index for case-insensitive email lookups
CREATE INDEX idx_lower_email ON users (lower(email));
```

---

## How to read EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE (what to look for)

- Seq Scan vs Index Scan vs Index Only Scan: Seq Scan reads full table.
- cost= (planner estimate): shows estimated startup and total cost — compare to actual times.
- rows= vs actual rows= (in Postgres: rows= vs actual rows=): big mismatches mean bad stats.
- Buffers/IO: look for lots of disk reads — consider caching, or a different plan.

Example snippet of EXPLAIN ANALYZE output and what it means:

```text
Index Scan using idx_events_user_id on events  (cost=0.29..12.34 rows=100 width=80) (actual time=0.10..0.20 rows=120 loops=1)
```
- Planner expected ~100 rows; actual 120 — good enough. Actual time shows fast index usage.

If you see: `Seq Scan on events (actual time=2000.0..2100.0)` that's a problem.

---

## Common pitfalls and how to avoid them

- Over-indexing: each index slows INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE and consumes disk. Only index columns used in WHERE/ORDER/GROUP.
- Wrong column order in composite indexes: index on (a,b) doesn't help queries filtering only on b.
- Low-cardinality columns: indexing a boolean or tiny enum is often useless (planner may still sequential scan).
- Forgotten functions: WHERE lower(email) = 'x' won't use index on email. Use expression index: `CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email));`
- Stale statistics: run ANALYZE or rely on autovacuum so planner has accurate row estimates.
- Assuming index always helps: sometimes a full table scan is faster for very large fraction reads.
- Index bloat: frequent updates can bloat indexes; run routine maintenance (VACUUM, REINDEX when necessary).

---

## Decision checklist (practical)

1. Identify slow queries: logs, monitoring (pg_stat_statements, slow query log).
2. Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE to see actual plan.
3. If Seq Scan and selective WHERE -> consider index on the predicate columns.
4. Consider composite idx for combined filters or ORDER BY to avoid sorting.
5. If query returns only indexed cols -> aim for index-only scan (covering index).
6. Re-run EXPLAIN ANALYZE and measure in staging with representative data.
7. Monitor writes: measure INSERT/UPDATE throughput after adding indexes.

---

## Example optimization workflow (mermaid)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Detect slow query] --> B[EXPLAIN ANALYZE]
  B --> C{Plan shows SeqScan?}
  C -- Yes --> D[Add index on filter cols]
  C -- No --> E[Check stats / rewrite query]
  D --> F[Test performance]
  E --> F
  F --> G[Confirm in prod & monitor]
```

---

## When NOT to add an index

- The predicate matches >~10-30% of table rows (depends on size & DB); sequential scan could be cheaper.
- Column has extremely low cardinality (booleans, tiny enums) and no additional limiting filters.
- Table is tiny — full scan is cheap and index overhead isn't worth it.

---

## Quick win tips

- Index columns used in JOIN, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY.
- Use LIMIT to reduce return size in UI queries and combine with proper ORDER BY + index.
- For pagination, avoid OFFSET for large pages; use keyset pagination (WHERE (col, id) < (last_col, last_id)).
- Keep stats fresh. In Postgres: `ANALYZE table_name;` or tune autovacuum.

---

## Final note

Indexing is both art and measurement. The right index can cut latency by orders of magnitude — but indexes are not free. Diagnose with EXPLAIN ANALYZE, test on representative data, and watch the write cost.
keyTakeaways: Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE to diagnose — don’t guess
Index the columns used in WHERE / JOIN / ORDER BY, and prefer composite indexes with proper column order
Balance read speed against write cost: fewer, targeted indexes often beat many broad ones
concept.codeExample:
-- Python example: measure query time against Postgres
import time
import psycopg2
conn = psycopg2.connect(dbname='mydb')
cur = conn.cursor()
cur.execute("EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM events WHERE user_id = %s", (12345,))
print('\n'.join(row[0] for row in cur.fetchall()))
# raw timing
start = time.time()
cur.execute("SELECT * FROM events WHERE user_id = %s", (12345,))
rows = cur.fetchall()
print('rows', len(rows), 'time', time.time() - start)
